         Introduce Markets on THB exposure — OWNER UNASSIGNED

reviews.name: Sophia Merrill
reviews.comment: The most-used prompt on my team and it is not close. It removes the job everyone puts off.

prompts.title: Pitchbook fact-check
prompts.description: Checks every number in a draft pitchbook against its source and flags anything unsupported.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual page-by-page number check
prompts.narrative: Nothing reaches a client that the deck cannot support.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.

tutorial.title: Fact-checking a deck before it ships

inputs.label: Source pack
inputs.note: Filings and research behind the numbers

guidelines: A flagged number is not a wrong number — it is one you must be able to source on the spot.
Update the footnote, not just the figure. Clients read footnotes.
Run this before the internal review, not after.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are quality-checking a client pitchbook at MUFG.

INPUT: {{DRAFT PITCHBOOK}}, {{SOURCE PACK}}

TASK
For every figure, chart label and claim in the deck, return:
| Page | Figure | Stated source | Found in source pack? | Discrepancy |

Then list the three highest-risk items to fix before the meeting.

CONSTRAINTS
- Mark UNSOURCED where no supporting document exists.
- Check that as-of dates match between the deck and the source.
- Do not correct a number; report the discrepancy and let a human decide.
prompts.sample_output:
FACT CHECK — 78 figures, 6 flags

p.12  "USD 4.2bn market size"  | source: sector note | FOUND, but 2024 vintage
p.19  "3rd largest by revenue" | source: none        | UNSOURCED
p.24  EBITDA margin 21.4%      | source: FY26 filing | DISCREPANCY: filing states 21.1% (reported vs adjusted)

HIGHEST RISK: p.19 — a ranking claim with no source

reviews.name: James Whitfield
reviews.comment: Caught a ranking claim on page 19 that nobody could source. That is a career-limiting slide if a client challenges it.

prompts.title: Client wallet share estimator
prompts.description: Estimates MUFG share of a client total banking wallet and where the gap sits by product.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual estimate built in a spreadsheet
prompts.narrative: Account plans start from a number rather than a feeling.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: This is an estimate built on public data and benchmarks — never present it to the client as fact.
State the confidence level; a wallet estimate without one is misleading in an account plan.
Do not combine it with information learned confidentially from another client.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are building an account plan at MUFG.

INPUT: {{MUFG REVENUE}}, {{CLIENT DISCLOSURES}}, {{WALLET BENCHMARKS}}

TASK
1. Estimate total client banking wallet, with the method stated
2. MUFG share overall and by product line
3. The two products with the largest absolute gap
4. Confidence level: high / medium / low, with the reason

CONSTRAINTS
- Show the estimation method and every assumption.
- Never present the estimate to a client as a fact.
- Where disclosure is thin, say LOW CONFIDENCE rather than narrowing the range.
prompts.sample_output:
WALLET ESTIMATE — MEDIUM CONFIDENCE

Estimated total wallet   USD 62–78m (benchmark method, sector fee ratios)
MUFG share               18–23%
Largest gaps             DCM underwriting (est. USD 14m, 0% share)
                         Cash management (est. USD 9m, ~8% share)

Method and assumptions listed in full below ...

reviews.name: Travis Fletcher
reviews.comment: Honest about its own uncertainty, which most wallet models are not. The confidence label keeps the account plan credible.

prompts.title: Financial spreading quality check
prompts.description: Checks a completed spread against the source statements and flags mapping errors before the memo is written.
prompts.repetition: Catches mapping errors that otherwise surface at committee
prompts.narrative: Errors are caught at the spread, not in front of the credit committee.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.

tutorial.title: Checking a spread before you trust it

guidelines: A flag is a question, not a correction. Re-map manually rather than accepting a suggestion.
Check consistency with the prior year spread — most errors are inconsistencies, not mistakes.
Restatements must be handled in the spread, not explained away in the memo.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a credit analyst validating a financial spread at MUFG.

INPUT: {{COMPLETED SPREAD}}, {{SOURCE STATEMENTS}}, {{PRIOR YEAR SPREAD}}

TASK
1. Reconcile every spread line to the source statement
2. Flag mapping differences, sign errors and missing notes
3. Compare treatment against the prior year spread for consistency
4. List any restatement or accounting policy change and its effect

OUTPUT
| Line | Spread value | Source value | Difference | Likely cause | Severity |

CONSTRAINTS
- Never silently correct a figure — report and let the analyst decide.
- Treat any unexplained difference above 2% as HIGH severity.
prompts.sample_output:
SPREAD RECONCILIATION — 4 flags

Other income   | 42.1 | 38.6 | +3.5 | disposal gain mapped to operating | HIGH
Lease liability| 0    | 210  | −210 | not mapped — IFRS 16 line missing  | HIGH
Inventory      | 88.4 | 88.4 | 0    | consistent with prior year        | —

POLICY CHANGE: revenue recognition restated in FY25 comparatives

reviews.name: Sarah Kendall
reviews.comment: The consistency check against last year is what makes this valuable. Most spread errors are drift, not blunders.

prompts.title: Industry risk section drafter
prompts.description: Writes the industry risk section of a credit memo from research and the borrower own competitive position.
prompts.repetition: Removes a repeated drafting task on every application
prompts.narrative: Industry sections stop being boilerplate copied from the last deal.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.

tutorial.title: Writing an industry section that says something

guidelines: The section must say something specific about this borrower, not the sector in general.
Every risk named needs a transmission mechanism to this borrower cash flow.
Do not reuse a section from a prior memo without re-running it — sector views move.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are drafting the industry risk section of a MUFG credit memo.

INPUT: {{SECTOR RESEARCH}}, {{BORROWER FILINGS}}
PEERS: {{PEER SET}}

TASK
Write 350 words covering:
1. Sector structure and where the borrower sits within it
2. The three risks most likely to affect this borrower's cash flow
3. For each, the transmission mechanism and the borrower's exposure
4. What would have to be true for the sector view to be wrong

CONSTRAINTS
- Generic sector commentary is not acceptable — anchor to this borrower.
- Cite the research source and date for every sector claim.
- Do not state a rating or a recommendation.
prompts.sample_output:
INDUSTRY RISK (draft, 350 words)

The borrower operates in the mid-tier segment of a sector where scale
increasingly determines margin. With 4% share against a top-three average
of 19%, it lacks the procurement leverage that has protected peer margins...

RISK 1  Input cost pass-through lag
  Transmission: 60% of contracts reprice annually, not quarterly
  Exposure: a 10% input move compresses EBITDA by an estimated 140bps ...

reviews.name: Martin Ashford
reviews.comment: The "what would have to be true for this view to be wrong" section is unusual and genuinely useful at committee.

prompts.title: Peer benchmarking table builder
prompts.description: Builds a like-for-like peer comparison table with the adjustments needed to make the numbers comparable.
prompts.repetition: Replaces manual normalisation across peer filings
prompts.narrative: Peer tables that survive the first challenge about comparability.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: Different reporting standards make raw comparison misleading — check every adjustment the prompt makes.
State the accounting basis in the table header; committee will ask.
A peer with a different fiscal year end needs calendarising before it belongs in the table.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a credit analyst building a peer table at MUFG.

INPUT: {{BORROWER FINANCIALS}}, {{PEER FINANCIALS}}
METRICS: {{METRICS REQUIRED}}

TASK
Build a comparison table with every figure normalised for comparability.
Show both the reported and the adjusted figure, and list each adjustment.

CONSTRAINTS
- State the accounting standard for each company.
- Calendarise any peer with a different fiscal year end and say so.
- Mark NOT COMPARABLE rather than forcing a metric that does not translate.
prompts.sample_output:
PEER TABLE — leverage and margin (all IFRS unless noted)

              Borrower   Peer A    Peer B (US GAAP)   Peer C
Net debt/EBITDA  2.4x     2.1x      1.9x*              3.6x
  *adjusted for operating lease capitalisation (+0.4x)
EBITDA margin    21.4%    24.1%     NOT COMPARABLE — segment reporting differs
Peer C calendarised from Mar-end to Dec-end

reviews.name: Julia Nolan
reviews.comment: The NOT COMPARABLE flag is better than a forced number. I have seen committee decisions made on peer tables that were quietly comparing different things.

prompts.title: Cash flow quality analysis
prompts.description: Separates recurring operating cash from one-offs and working capital swings across three years.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual three-year cash flow rebuild
prompts.narrative: Distinguishes cash the borrower generates from cash it borrowed or released once.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: Maintenance capex is rarely disclosed — where you estimate it, label the estimate in the memo.
A working capital release is not earnings. The prompt separates them; make sure the memo does too.
Cross-check against the cash conversion in the spreading tool.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a credit analyst assessing cash flow quality at MUFG.

INPUT: {{CASH FLOW STATEMENTS}}, {{NOTES}}, {{CAPEX BREAKDOWN}}

TASK
1. Rebuild operating cash flow excluding one-off items, listing each
2. Isolate the working capital contribution year by year
3. Estimate maintenance capex and free cash flow after it
4. State whether cash generation is improving on a like-for-like basis

CONSTRAINTS
- Label every estimate as ESTIMATE with its basis.
- Never treat a working capital release as recurring cash generation.
- If the notes do not support a one-off classification, leave it in.
prompts.sample_output:
CASH FLOW QUALITY — FY24 to FY26

Reported OCF        412    380    455
One-offs removed    (48)   (12)   (96)   [disposal proceeds, tax refund]
Working capital     +88    (34)   +141   ← FY26 driven by payables extension
Underlying OCF      276    402    218

Maintenance capex   ESTIMATE 180 (basis: depreciation less growth capex)
Underlying FCF      96     222    38     — deteriorating like-for-like

reviews.name: Paige Norton
reviews.comment: The payables extension in FY26 would have been easy to miss in the headline number. This is the analysis that changes a credit view.

prompts.title: Working capital cycle diagnostic
prompts.description: Breaks down the cash conversion cycle and identifies which component is driving a deterioration.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual component-by-component walk
prompts.narrative: Points at the specific line causing the cash squeeze rather than the symptom.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: Use quarterly data where you can — annual figures hide seasonal swings entirely.
A lengthening payables cycle can mean supplier financing rather than negotiating strength. Check.
Compare against sector norms before calling a cycle length a problem.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a credit analyst diagnosing working capital at MUFG.

INPUT: {{BALANCE SHEET HISTORY}}, {{REVENUE AND COGS}}, {{SECTOR NORMS}}

TASK
1. DSO, DIO, DPO and the cash conversion cycle by period
2. Which component drives the movement, quantified in cash terms
3. Whether the movement is seasonal, structural or a financing decision
4. Two questions to put to management

CONSTRAINTS
- State the formula used for each ratio.
- Distinguish a supplier financing programme from genuine terms extension.
- Where only annual data exists, warn that seasonality is not visible.
prompts.sample_output:
CASH CONVERSION CYCLE

           FY24   FY25   FY26
DSO         62     64     71    ← driver, +USD 84m cash absorbed
DIO         88     91     89
DPO         (54)   (58)   (79)  ← possible supplier financing, CONFIRM
CCC         96     97     81

WARNING: annual data only — seasonal peak not visible
QUESTIONS: 1. Has collections policy changed in any major market?

reviews.name: Sarah Kendall
reviews.comment: The supplier financing flag on DPO is the right instinct. An extended payables cycle can look like strength and be the opposite.

prompts.title: Rating rationale drafter
prompts.description: Drafts the rationale supporting an internal rating recommendation, mapped to the rating methodology.
prompts.repetition: Removes a repeated drafting task on every rating action
prompts.narrative: Rating rationales trace to the methodology rather than to analyst instinct.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.

tutorial.title: Writing a rationale that maps to the methodology

guidelines: The rationale supports your rating — it does not produce one. Decide first, then draft.
Every factor score must trace to a methodology section reference.
Where you override the model output, the reason belongs in the rationale, prominently.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are drafting an internal rating rationale at MUFG.

INPUT: {{FINANCIAL ANALYSIS}}, {{RATING METHODOLOGY}}
PROPOSED: {{PROPOSED RATING}}

TASK
Draft the rationale mapping each methodology factor to the evidence:
| Factor | Methodology reference | Score | Evidence | Weight |

Then a 250-word narrative supporting the proposed rating, and a
paragraph on what would move the rating up or down.

CONSTRAINTS
- Every score carries a methodology section reference.
- Any override of the model output must be stated explicitly with a reason.
- Do not propose a rating; support the one given.
prompts.sample_output:
RATING RATIONALE — proposed BBB− (internal scale 7)

Business risk     §3.2   Moderate   4% share, limited pricing power
Financial risk    §4.1   Moderate   Net leverage 2.4x, coverage 4.1x
Country risk      §5.4   Low        90% of revenue in investment-grade markets
Override: model output 6; downgraded one notch for customer concentration
(top 3 = 54% of revenue), methodology §3.6 permits this adjustment.

reviews.name: Martin Ashford
reviews.comment: Forcing the override reason into the rationale is good practice. Overrides are where rating discipline usually breaks down.

prompts.title: Contractor counterparty risk note
prompts.description: Assesses the EPC contractor behind a project and what happens to the deal if it fails.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual contractor financial review
prompts.narrative: The contractor is usually the weakest link, and now it is assessed like one.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Contractor accounts are often stale or unaudited — state the vintage in the note.
Assess replacement cost and delay, not just probability of failure.
Parent guarantees are only as strong as the parent; check whether it is rated.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a structured finance credit analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{CONTRACTOR FINANCIALS}}, {{EPC CONTRACT}}
PROJECT: {{PROJECT DETAILS}}

TASK
1. Contractor financial condition, with the accounts vintage stated
2. Order book concentration and this project's share of it
3. Security package: bonds, retentions, LDs, parent guarantee strength
4. Replacement scenario: cost, delay and impact on the DSCR profile
5. Two mitigants worth negotiating before financial close

CONSTRAINTS
- State the age and audit status of the contractor accounts.
- Assess the guarantor separately; a guarantee from an unrated parent is not credit support.
- Quantify the replacement delay in months, not qualitatively.
prompts.sample_output:
CONTRACTOR ASSESSMENT

Accounts vintage   FY25, audited, 14 months old — DATED
Order book         Project is 31% of current book — high dependency
Security           10% performance bond, 5% retention, LDs capped at 15%
Parent guarantee   Unrated holding company — LIMITED CREDIT SUPPORT

REPLACEMENT SCENARIO
Cost +12–18% | Delay 7–11 months | Minimum DSCR falls to 1.04x

reviews.name: Peter Lawson
reviews.comment: The unrated-parent point is one people wave through constantly. Good that it refuses to treat it as credit support.

prompts.title: Offtake agreement risk extract
prompts.description: Pulls the terms that determine revenue certainty out of an offtake or PPA and flags the weak ones.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a full manual read of a long-form offtake
prompts.narrative: Revenue risk is understood before the model assumes it away.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.

tutorial.title: Reading an offtake for what it does not say

guidelines: Check that every model revenue assumption is actually supported by a clause.
Termination and step-in rights matter more than headline tenor.
Any clause requiring legal interpretation goes to Legal, not into the memo.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a project finance credit analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{OFFTAKE AGREEMENT}}, {{FINANCIAL MODEL}}

TASK
Extract every term affecting revenue certainty:
| Clause | Term | Effect on revenue | Model assumption | Aligned? |

Cover: tenor, volume commitment, price mechanism, indexation, curtailment,
force majeure, change in law, termination and step-in rights.

CONSTRAINTS
- Quote the clause reference for every extraction.
- Flag MODEL MISMATCH where the model assumes more than the contract gives.
- Mark LEGAL REVIEW where the drafting is ambiguous.
prompts.sample_output:
OFFTAKE EXTRACT — 9 terms, 2 mismatches

cl. 4.1  Tenor 15 years, offtaker termination right at year 10 on 24m notice
         Model assumes 15 years flat — MODEL MISMATCH
cl. 7.3  Price indexed to CPI, capped at 3% p.a.
         Model assumes uncapped CPI — MODEL MISMATCH, material post-2031
cl. 11.2 Curtailment compensation — LEGAL REVIEW, "reasonable endeavours"

reviews.name: Michael Barrett
reviews.comment: Two model mismatches on a live deal, both material after year 10. This is the prompt that pays for the programme.

prompts.title: Construction progress review note
prompts.description: Turns a lender technical adviser report into the construction section of a monitoring memo.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual read of a monthly LTA report
prompts.narrative: Slippage is visible in the monitoring memo the month it happens.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: Compare against the prior month — a single report shows status, two show direction.
Physical progress and cost progress diverging is the early warning worth escalating.
The LTA opinion is the record; do not paraphrase it into something softer.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are monitoring a project finance construction phase at MUFG.

INPUT: {{LTA REPORT}}, {{PRIOR MONTH}}, {{MILESTONE SCHEDULE}}

TASK
1. Physical progress versus plan, and versus last month
2. Cost progress versus plan — flag divergence from physical progress
3. Milestones at risk, with the contractual consequence of each
4. LTA opinions and qualifications, quoted, not paraphrased
5. What to escalate this month

CONSTRAINTS
- Quote LTA qualifications verbatim, briefly.
- Never soften a technical opinion.
- Where the report does not address a milestone, say so.
prompts.sample_output:
CONSTRUCTION REVIEW — Month 14

Physical progress   61% vs 66% plan (last month: 55% vs 58%) — slippage widening
Cost progress       68% drawn — DIVERGENCE of 7pts against physical
Milestones at risk  Grid connection (M18) — 6 week float remaining

LTA qualification: notes commissioning sequence "not yet fully defined"
ESCALATE: cost/physical divergence, two consecutive months

reviews.name: Emily Preston
reviews.comment: The divergence trend across two months is the signal. One month of it means nothing.

prompts.title: Sponsor track record summary
prompts.description: Assembles a sponsor delivery history from public sources and prior MUFG deals.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual search across past deal files
prompts.narrative: Sponsor claims get checked against what they actually delivered.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Separate what the sponsor delivered from what an affiliate delivered.
A project completed late is not a failure — record the reason, not just the delay.
Internal deal history is confidential to the bank; keep it out of any client-facing material.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are conducting sponsor diligence at MUFG.

INPUT: {{SPONSOR PRESENTATION}}, {{PUBLIC RECORDS}}, {{MUFG DEAL HISTORY}}

TASK
1. Projects delivered, with role: sponsor, co-sponsor or affiliate
2. Delivery record: on time, delayed, abandoned — with reasons where known
3. Claims in the presentation that public records do not support
4. MUFG's own experience, where a prior relationship exists

CONSTRAINTS
- Distinguish the sponsor entity from affiliates and funds under management.
- Mark UNVERIFIED where only the sponsor's own material supports a claim.
- Internal deal history stays internal.
prompts.sample_output:
SPONSOR TRACK RECORD

Delivered as sponsor      6 projects, 4 on time, 2 delayed (grid, permitting)
Delivered as affiliate    9 projects — claimed as own in presentation p.7
UNVERIFIED CLAIM          "zero cost overruns across portfolio" — no public support

MUFG experience: 2 prior facilities, both performing (internal, do not share)

reviews.name: Rebecca Stone
reviews.comment: The affiliate-versus-sponsor distinction catches a very common presentation habit.

prompts.title: LBO capital structure sanity check
prompts.description: Tests whether a proposed LBO structure can service its debt under the sponsor own base case.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual rebuild of the sponsor model
prompts.narrative: Structures that only work on the sponsor assumptions are exposed early.
prompts.risk_note: Deal-sensitive or control-facing. Restricted to a cleared team; every run is logged and reviewable by Compliance.
guidelines: Deal-team only until the commitment is public.
Test the sponsor case first, then your own — the difference is the negotiation.
Never rely on a sponsor-supplied model without rebuilding the debt schedule.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a leveraged finance credit analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{SPONSOR MODEL}}, {{SECTOR PRECEDENTS}}
STRUCTURE: {{PROPOSED STRUCTURE}}

TASK
1. Opening and exit leverage against sector precedent
2. Cash interest cover in each year of the sponsor base case
3. The first year where free cash flow after debt service turns negative
4. Deleveraging path: how much comes from EBITDA growth versus cash sweep
5. The assumption the whole structure depends on

CONSTRAINTS
- Rebuild the debt schedule; do not take the sponsor's on trust.
- State whether covenants are maintenance or incurrence.
- Identify the single assumption with the largest effect on serviceability.
prompts.sample_output:
LBO SANITY CHECK

Opening leverage   5.8x vs sector precedent median 5.1x — ABOVE
Cash interest cover 1.9x FY1, trough 1.6x FY3
FCF after debt service turns negative: none in base case
Deleveraging       72% from EBITDA growth, 28% from sweep

LOAD-BEARING ASSUMPTION: 9% EBITDA CAGR. At 5%, exit leverage is 4.6x not 3.4x

reviews.name: Christopher Wade
reviews.comment: Naming the single load-bearing assumption is the most useful line in the output. That is the thing to negotiate around.

prompts.title: Debt schedule reconstruction
prompts.description: Rebuilds a complete debt maturity schedule from filings when the company does not disclose one clearly.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual trawl through footnotes
prompts.narrative: The maturity wall becomes visible even when the company would rather it were not.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.

tutorial.title: Rebuilding a debt schedule from footnotes

guidelines: Post-balance-sheet issuance is the most commonly missed item — always check the interims.
Undrawn committed facilities are not debt, but they belong in the liquidity picture.
Where currency is mixed, state the translation rate and date.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are reconstructing a borrower's debt profile at MUFG.

INPUT: {{ANNUAL REPORT}}, {{BOND PROSPECTUSES}}, {{INTERIM STATEMENTS}}

TASK
Build a complete debt schedule:
| Instrument | Currency | Amount | Rate | Maturity | Secured? | Source reference |

Then a maturity profile by year and a note on refinancing concentration.

CONSTRAINTS
- Cite the note or page for every instrument.
- Include post-balance-sheet issuance and say where it came from.
- State the FX translation rate and date for any conversion.
- Mark INCOMPLETE where disclosure does not permit a full reconstruction.
prompts.sample_output:
DEBT SCHEDULE — 11 instruments, USD 2.14bn equivalent

2027 Notes    USD 750m  4.25%  Jun 2027  Unsecured  (AR note 22)
Term loan B   EUR 400m  E+375  Sep 2029  Secured    (AR note 22)
Bilateral     JPY 20bn  0.9%   Mar 2028  Unsecured  (interim, p.14 — issued post year-end)

MATURITY WALL: 2027 carries 41% of total. FX at 31 Dec 25 rates.

reviews.name: Julia Nolan
reviews.comment: Caught a post-year-end bilateral that the annual report alone would have missed entirely.

prompts.title: Early warning signal scan
prompts.description: Scans recent filings, news and account behaviour for the signals that usually precede a downgrade.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual monthly review across the book
prompts.narrative: Problems surface while there is still time to restructure rather than recover.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: A signal is not a decision. Two or more correlated signals warrant a watchlist discussion.
Account behaviour data is highly confidential — it stays inside Credit.
Do not raise a signal with the client relationship team before Credit has reviewed it.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are monitoring a borrower portfolio at MUFG.

INPUT: {{LATEST FILINGS}}, {{ACCOUNT BEHAVIOUR}}, {{PUBLIC NEWS}}

TASK
Scan for early warning signals across four categories:
financial, behavioural, governance and market.

For each signal found: evidence, category, strength (weak/moderate/strong),
and whether it correlates with any other signal present.

CONSTRAINTS
- Never report a signal without its supporting evidence.
- Correlated signals must be grouped, not listed separately.
- Do not recommend a rating action; this is detection, not decision.
prompts.sample_output:
EARLY WARNING SCAN — 5 signals, 1 correlated cluster

CLUSTER (moderate–strong)
  • Revolver utilisation up from 40% to 88% over two quarters (behavioural)
  • Payables days extended by 21 days (financial)
  • CFO departure announced, no successor named (governance)
  → These three correlate. Recommend watchlist discussion.

ISOLATED (weak): sector news coverage, auditor unchanged

reviews.name: Sarah Kendall
reviews.comment: Grouping correlated signals is what separates this from an alert list. Three weak signals pointing the same way is a strong signal.

prompts.title: Annual review memo refresh
prompts.description: Updates last year credit memo with current financials and marks every change for review.
prompts.repetition: Removes a full rewrite on every annual review
prompts.narrative: Reviews start from last year thinking instead of a blank page.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.

tutorial.title: Refreshing a memo without losing the argument

guidelines: Every carried-forward paragraph is your responsibility. Read it, do not skim it.
Conditions from the prior approval must be addressed explicitly, not deleted.
Where the prior view no longer holds, rewrite the paragraph rather than adjusting the number.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are refreshing an annual credit review at MUFG.

INPUT: {{PRIOR MEMO}}, {{CURRENT FINANCIALS}}, {{FACILITY LIST}}

TASK
Produce an updated memo where every change is marked:
[UPDATED] figure or fact refreshed
[CHANGED VIEW] prior analysis no longer holds — needs rewriting
[UNCHANGED] carried forward, still supported
[CONDITION] prior approval condition, with its current status

CONSTRAINTS
- Never carry forward a conclusion whose supporting number has moved materially.
- Flag every prior condition, including satisfied ones.
- Do not delete prior analysis; mark it for rewrite instead.
prompts.sample_output:
MEMO REFRESH — 34 paragraphs, 11 marked

[CHANGED VIEW] §4.2 "stable margin profile" — margin fell 180bps, rewrite
[UPDATED]      §3.1 revenue, EBITDA, leverage figures refreshed to FY26
[CONDITION]    Quarterly management accounts — SATISFIED, received Q1–Q3
[CONDITION]    Capex limited to USD 200m — STATUS UNCLEAR, schedule missing
[UNCHANGED]    §5.4 country risk assessment, still supported

reviews.name: Martin Ashford
reviews.comment: The [CHANGED VIEW] marker stops the copy-paste annual review, which is exactly the failure mode this is meant to prevent.

prompts.title: Guarantor support assessment
prompts.description: Assesses whether a parent guarantee provides real credit support, and how much.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual guarantor financial review
prompts.narrative: A guarantee is treated as credit support only when it actually is.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: A guarantee from a weaker entity than the borrower is not credit support. Say so plainly.
Check enforceability in the guarantor jurisdiction with Legal before relying on it.
Structural subordination survives a guarantee — check where the assets actually sit.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are assessing guarantor support at MUFG.

INPUT: {{GUARANTEE DOCUMENT}}, {{GUARANTOR FINANCIALS}}, {{GROUP STRUCTURE}}

TASK
1. Guarantee type: full, limited, several, letter of comfort
2. Guarantor standalone financial strength versus the borrower
3. Where the group's assets and cash actually sit
4. Enforceability considerations by jurisdiction
5. Conclusion: material support, limited support, or presentational only

CONSTRAINTS
- A letter of comfort is not a guarantee. Never treat it as one.
- Flag structural subordination explicitly.
- Route all enforceability questions to Legal as LEGAL REVIEW.
prompts.sample_output:
GUARANTOR ASSESSMENT

Type              Limited guarantee, capped at USD 300m of USD 500m facility
Guarantor strength Holdco, no operating assets — WEAKER than borrower
Asset location    92% of group assets sit at opcos below the borrower
Structural subordination: MATERIAL

CONCLUSION: presentational only. LEGAL REVIEW — enforceability in two markets.

reviews.name: Julia Nolan
reviews.comment: "Presentational only" is a phrase more credit memos need. This one is not shy about saying it.

prompts.title: Sector downturn precedent finder
prompts.description: Finds how comparable borrowers behaved in the last sector downturn and what predicted survival.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual search through historical cases
prompts.narrative: Stress assumptions grounded in what actually happened last time.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: A precedent is not a forecast. Structures and markets change between cycles.
State how comparable each precedent company actually is — most are only partly so.
Use the findings to set stress assumptions, not to conclude an outcome.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a credit analyst studying downturn precedent at MUFG.

INPUT: {{HISTORICAL DATA}}, {{BORROWER PROFILE}}
PERIOD: {{DOWNTURN DEFINITION}}

TASK
1. Comparable borrowers in the defined downturn, with comparability rated
2. What happened to revenue, margin and leverage, by quartile
3. The financial characteristics that separated survivors from failures
4. Where this borrower sits on each of those characteristics
5. Three stress assumptions the precedent supports

CONSTRAINTS
- Rate comparability high / medium / low for each precedent, with the reason.
- Distinguish company failure from restructuring and from acquisition.
- Do not conclude an outcome for this borrower.
prompts.sample_output:
DOWNTURN PRECEDENT — 2020–21, 14 comparable borrowers

Revenue decline    median −18%, worst quartile −34%
Margin compression median 320bps
SURVIVAL FACTORS   liquidity headroom >9 months, leverage <3.5x entering,
                   no maturity inside 18 months

THIS BORROWER      liquidity 11 months ✓ | leverage 2.4x ✓ | maturity 14 months ✗

SUPPORTED STRESS   revenue −20%, margin −300bps, no refinancing access 12m

reviews.name: Paige Norton
reviews.comment: The survival-factor framing is more useful than a simple percentage stress. It tells you which stress actually matters.

prompts.title: Country risk limit review
prompts.description: Reviews exposure against country limits and explains what is driving any move toward the cap.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual quarterly limit walk
prompts.narrative: Limit pressure is explained before it becomes a breach conversation.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Aggregate above the single-obligor threshold before upload.
Contingent and contractual exposure must be shown alongside drawn, never instead of it.
Any recommendation to change a limit goes through the Country Risk forum.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a country risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{EXPOSURE DATA}}, {{LIMIT FRAMEWORK}}
PERIOD: {{REVIEW PERIOD}}

TASK
1. Exposure versus limit by country, drawn and contractual
2. Countries above 80% utilisation, ranked
3. What drove each move: new business, drawdown, FX or rating migration
4. Countries where the limit no longer reflects the risk environment

CONSTRAINTS
- Show drawn and contractual exposure separately throughout.
- Attribute every move to a cause; unexplained movement is a data quality issue.
- Do not propose limit changes; identify the cases for the forum.
prompts.sample_output:
COUNTRY LIMIT REVIEW — Q2 2026

Country A   USD 4.1bn drawn / 6.8bn contractual | 94% of limit
  Driver: FX translation (+3pts), new facilities (+6pts)
Country B   USD 2.2bn / 3.0bn | 87% of limit
  Driver: drawdown on existing commitments, no new business
Country C   72% — UNEXPLAINED movement of 4pts, data quality issue raised

reviews.name: Thomas Bradley
reviews.comment: The requirement to attribute every move surfaces data quality problems that would otherwise be smoothed over.

prompts.title: Counterparty exposure summary
prompts.description: Aggregates derivative and settlement exposure to a counterparty group across desks and products.
prompts.repetition: Replaces manual aggregation across three systems
prompts.narrative: The bank sees a counterparty as one exposure, not six desk positions.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Netting only applies where a legally enforceable agreement exists — check, do not assume.
Group aggregation must follow the connected-counterparty definition, not the commercial one.
Collateral held reduces exposure only where the CSA permits it in that jurisdiction.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a counterparty credit risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{EXPOSURE DATA}}, {{NETTING STATUS}}, {{GROUP STRUCTURE}}

TASK
1. Gross and net exposure by product and desk
2. Netting benefit, and where it is not legally enforceable
3. Collateral held and the residual uncollateralised exposure
4. Group aggregation under the connected counterparty definition
5. The largest single driver of net exposure

CONSTRAINTS
- Apply netting only where enforceability is confirmed; otherwise show gross.
- State the collateral haircut applied and its source.
- Follow the regulatory connected-counterparty definition, not the client hierarchy.
prompts.sample_output:
COUNTERPARTY EXPOSURE — Group total

Gross exposure       USD 1.84bn across 4 desks
Netting benefit      USD 1.12bn — of which USD 90m NOT ENFORCEABLE (one entity)
Collateral held      USD 480m after haircuts (CSA schedule, 8% haircut)
Net uncollateralised USD 330m

LARGEST DRIVER: cross-currency swap book, single desk, 61% of net

reviews.name: Yvonne Hadley
reviews.comment: The unenforceable netting flag is exactly the sort of thing that gets assumed away in a spreadsheet.

prompts.title: Climate transition risk mapper
prompts.description: Maps portfolio exposure to transition risk by sector and policy scenario.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual sector-by-sector mapping exercise
prompts.narrative: Transition exposure becomes a number the risk committee can act on.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.

tutorial.title: Mapping transition risk across a book

inputs.label: Portfolio exposure by sector
inputs.note: Aggregated, with NACE or SIC codes

guidelines: Scenario outputs are indicative and must not be used for regulatory disclosure without the sanctioned platform.
State the scenario, vintage and provider on every output — these change frequently.
Sector codes are a proxy for activity, not the activity itself. Note the limitation.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a climate risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{PORTFOLIO EXPOSURE}}, {{EMISSIONS DATA}}
SCENARIO: {{TRANSITION SCENARIO}}

TASK
1. Exposure by transition risk tier: high, moderate, low
2. The three sub-sectors carrying most exposure in the high tier
3. Indicative credit impact pathway under the scenario, by decade
4. Where sector coding is too coarse to give a reliable answer

CONSTRAINTS
- State the scenario name, provider and vintage in the output header.
- Mark PROXY wherever activity is inferred from a sector code.
- Indicative only — not for regulatory disclosure.
prompts.sample_output:
TRANSITION RISK MAP — NGFS Net Zero 2050 (v4.2, 2025)

High tier      USD 18.4bn (14% of book)
  Top sub-sectors: thermal coal logistics, refining, cement
Moderate       USD 41.2bn (31%)
Low            USD 72.9bn (55%)

PROXY WARNING: 22% of high-tier exposure classified by sector code only
INDICATIVE — not for Pillar 3 disclosure

reviews.name: Stephanie Lambert
reviews.comment: The proxy warning is important. A lot of climate analysis quietly rests on sector codes doing more work than they can.

prompts.title: Single name concentration alert
prompts.description: Identifies where exposure to one borrower group has grown past the level the framework intends.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual monthly concentration check
prompts.narrative: Single-name build-up is visible before it becomes a regulatory conversation.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Group aggregation must use the regulatory connected-counterparty test.
Report against both internal appetite and the regulatory large exposure limit — they differ.
Any exposure approaching the regulatory limit goes to the Head of Portfolio Risk the same day.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a portfolio risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{GROUP EXPOSURE}}, {{CAPITAL BASE}}, {{LARGE EXPOSURE FRAMEWORK}}

TASK
1. Top 20 obligor groups by exposure as a percentage of eligible capital
2. Position against internal appetite and the regulatory limit, separately
3. Groups where exposure grew more than 20% in the period, with the cause
4. Anything within 10% of a regulatory threshold — flagged for same-day escalation

CONSTRAINTS
- Use the regulatory connected-counterparty definition for grouping.
- Show internal and regulatory positions separately; never blend them.
- Include contractual as well as drawn exposure in the regulatory measure.
prompts.sample_output:
SINGLE NAME CONCENTRATION — top 20

Group 1   18.2% of eligible capital | internal appetite 20% | reg limit 25%
Group 2   14.6% | grew 26% this quarter — cause: new bridge commitment
Group 3   22.9% ⚠ WITHIN 10% OF REGULATORY LIMIT — escalate today

Regulatory measure includes undrawn commitments.

reviews.name: Thomas Bradley
reviews.comment: Keeping internal appetite and the regulatory limit separate matters. Blending them is how banks talk themselves into a breach.

prompts.title: Stress scenario narrative writer
prompts.description: Turns stress test output into the narrative the risk committee and the regulator expect to read.
prompts.repetition: Removes a repeated drafting task each stress cycle
prompts.narrative: Stress results are explained, not just tabulated.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Only results from the sanctioned platform may be written up for committee.
Explain the transmission mechanism; a table of losses without causation will be sent back.
Compare against the prior cycle and explain the difference, including methodology changes.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are writing up stress test results at MUFG.

INPUT: {{STRESS OUTPUT}}, {{SCENARIO DEFINITION}}, {{PRIOR CYCLE}}

TASK
1. Headline results: capital ratio path, peak-to-trough, loss composition
2. Transmission: how the scenario becomes losses, portfolio by portfolio
3. Comparison with the prior cycle, separating portfolio change from methodology change
4. The three portfolios driving the outcome
5. A 400-word committee narrative

CONSTRAINTS
- Every number must trace to the sanctioned platform output.
- Separate portfolio effects from methodology or model changes explicitly.
- No mitigating management actions unless they are board-approved.
prompts.sample_output:
STRESS RESULTS — Adverse scenario, 2026 cycle

CET1 path      13.8% → trough 9.4% (Y2) → 10.6% (Y3)
Peak-to-trough 440bps, against 380bps in the prior cycle
Of the 60bps deterioration: 35bps portfolio mix, 25bps model recalibration

TRANSMISSION  Unemployment path drives retail impairment in Y1–2; the
corporate effect lags by three quarters through rating migration ...

reviews.name: Laura Whitman
reviews.comment: Splitting portfolio effects from methodology changes is the first question the committee asks every single cycle. Good that it is built in.

prompts.title: Risk appetite breach explainer
prompts.description: Explains a risk appetite breach: what moved, why, and what the options are.
prompts.repetition: Replaces an ad hoc write-up each time a metric breaches
prompts.narrative: Breaches reach governance with a cause attached, not just a red cell.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: State the breach plainly. Softening language in a governance paper is a control failure.
Attribute the movement to a cause before proposing any action.
Where remediation requires a business decision, name the accountable executive.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a risk analyst reporting an appetite breach at MUFG.

INPUT: {{APPETITE DASHBOARD}}, {{METRIC HISTORY}}
BREACH: {{BREACHED METRIC}}

TASK
1. The breach: metric, threshold, current value, date first breached
2. Trend: was this sudden or a build-up over months
3. Cause attribution, quantified where possible
4. Options: remediate, transfer, accept with rationale — with owners
5. What happens if no action is taken this quarter

CONSTRAINTS
- Use plain, direct language. Do not soften the description of a breach.
- Attribute the cause before proposing action.
- Name an accountable owner for every option.
prompts.sample_output:
APPETITE BREACH — sector concentration, commercial real estate

Threshold      12% of book | Current 13.4% | First breached 30 Jun 2026
Trend          Build-up over 5 months, not a step change
Cause          68% drawdown on existing commitments, 32% book contraction elsewhere

OPTIONS
1. Remediate — slow new origination (Head of CRE, 2 quarters)
2. Transfer — synthetic risk transfer (Treasury, 3 quarters, cost implication)
3. Accept — requires Board Risk Committee, rationale not currently supported

IF NO ACTION: exposure reaches 14.1% by year end on committed drawdowns alone

reviews.name: Laura Whitman
reviews.comment: The "if no action" line is the one that gets decisions made. Without it a breach paper just sits there.

prompts.title: ICAAP section drafter
prompts.description: Drafts an ICAAP section from the underlying analysis, in the structure the regulator expects.
prompts.repetition: Removes a full drafting cycle from the ICAAP timetable
prompts.narrative: ICAAP drafting starts from structure rather than from a blank template.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Prior-year text may only be carried forward where the underlying analysis still supports it.
Every quantitative statement needs a traceable source; the regulator will ask for the workings.
Supervisory feedback from the last cycle must be addressed explicitly in the relevant section.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are drafting an ICAAP section at MUFG.

INPUT: {{UNDERLYING ANALYSIS}}, {{PRIOR ICAAP}}
SECTION: {{SECTION REQUIRED}}

TASK
Draft the section following the required structure. For each statement:
mark [NEW], [CARRIED FORWARD] or [UPDATED], and give the source.

Then list every point of supervisory feedback from the prior cycle that
this section must address, and whether the draft addresses it.

CONSTRAINTS
- Carry forward prior text only where current analysis supports it.
- Every number carries a traceable source reference.
- Flag UNSUPPORTED where the analysis does not evidence a statement.
prompts.sample_output:
ICAAP SECTION 4 — Credit risk capital adequacy

[UPDATED]         Economic capital of USD 8.2bn (source: EC model v9.1, Jun 26)
[CARRIED FORWARD] Methodology description, §4.2 — unchanged, still supported
[NEW]             Climate transition overlay, USD 340m
[UNSUPPORTED]     "conservative calibration" — no calibration evidence attached

SUPERVISORY FEEDBACK 2025
 • Concentration methodology detail — ADDRESSED in §4.5
 • Model validation independence — NOT ADDRESSED in this section

reviews.name: Stephanie Lambert
reviews.comment: Tracking supervisory feedback section by section is the part people get wrong. Very glad this enforces it.

prompts.title: Regulatory reporting reconciliation
prompts.description: Reconciles a regulatory return against the source ledger and explains every difference.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual line-by-line reconciliation
prompts.narrative: Return differences are explained before the regulator asks about them.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: An unexplained difference is a finding, not a rounding. Never close one without a cause.
Definitional differences between accounting and regulatory scope must be documented, not netted.
Finance signs off the reconciliation; this prompt prepares it.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are reconciling a regulatory return at MUFG.

INPUT: {{REGULATORY RETURN}}, {{SOURCE LEDGER}}, {{PRIOR PERIOD}}

TASK
Line by line, return:
| Return line | Return value | Ledger value | Difference | Cause | Documented? |

Classify each cause: definitional, timing, scope, data quality, unexplained.
Then list every unexplained difference above the materiality threshold.

CONSTRAINTS
- Never net differences against each other.
- Definitional differences must reference the rule that creates them.
- UNEXPLAINED is a valid answer; do not manufacture a cause.
prompts.sample_output:
RECONCILIATION — 46 lines, 7 differences

Line 12  Return 4,182 | Ledger 4,205 | −23 | definitional (reg scope excludes
         intragroup, CRR Art. 113) | DOCUMENTED
Line 27  Return 918   | Ledger 946   | −28 | timing, month-end cut-off | DOCUMENTED
Line 33  Return 2,104 | Ledger 2,151 | −47 | UNEXPLAINED — above threshold

reviews.name: David Carver
reviews.comment: The refusal to manufacture a cause is the right behaviour. An unexplained difference should stay unexplained until someone explains it.

prompts.title: Consultation paper response drafter
prompts.description: Drafts a response to a regulatory consultation, grounded in how the proposal affects MUFG specifically.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual first draft for each consultation
prompts.narrative: The bank responds to consultations that would otherwise pass without comment.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Responses are institutional positions. Regulatory Affairs owns the final text and the submission.
Ground every argument in a quantified impact on MUFG rather than in principle alone.
Never criticise a supervisor; argue the proposal, not the intent.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are drafting a consultation response for MUFG.

INPUT: {{CONSULTATION PAPER}}, {{IMPACT ANALYSIS}}
POSITION: {{AGREED POSITION}}

TASK
For each consultation question:
1. The proposal in one sentence
2. MUFG's position: support, support with modification, or oppose
3. The quantified impact supporting that position
4. A specific alternative where we oppose
5. Any implementation timing concern

CONSTRAINTS
- Every position must be supported by a quantified impact.
- Propose an alternative wherever we oppose; objection alone is not a response.
- Professional register throughout; argue the proposal, never the supervisor.
prompts.sample_output:
CONSULTATION RESPONSE — draft

Q4  Proposal: 10-year loss data history for operational risk capital
    Position: SUPPORT WITH MODIFICATION
    Impact: 3 of 7 acquired entities have 6–8 years; full compliance
            requires reconstruction at an estimated 4,200 person-hours
    Alternative: transitional treatment for entities acquired post-2020
    Timing: 18 months insufficient; 30 months proposed

reviews.name: Thomas Bradley
reviews.comment: Insisting on an alternative wherever we oppose makes the response constructive. Regulators discount pure objection.

prompts.title: Model validation finding summariser
prompts.description: Turns a model validation report into a tracked finding list with owners and remediation dates.
prompts.repetition: Replaces manual extraction into the findings tracker
prompts.narrative: Validation findings reach the tracker complete, with owners attached.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: A finding cannot be closed on the basis of this summary. Model Risk Management closes findings.
Check for duplicates against the existing tracker before adding.
Severity comes from the validation report, not from the model owner view of it.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are processing a model validation report at MUFG.

INPUT: {{VALIDATION REPORT}}, {{FINDINGS TRACKER}}

TASK
Extract every finding:
| Ref | Finding | Severity (as stated) | Model component | Owner | Due date | Duplicate? |

Then list findings that block continued model use, and any where the
report states a severity the model owner has disputed.

CONSTRAINTS
- Severity is taken from the validation report, never adjusted.
- Flag DUPLICATE where a matching open finding already exists.
- Quote the report where the finding restricts model use.
prompts.sample_output:
VALIDATION FINDINGS — 12 extracted, 2 duplicates

V-2026-041  High    PD calibration sample excludes 2020–21 | Owner: Quant | Q4 26
V-2026-042  Medium  Documentation of override policy incomplete | DUPLICATE of V-2025-118
V-2026-047  High    Backtesting frequency below policy — RESTRICTS USE
            Report states use should be limited pending remediation

reviews.name: Laura Whitman
reviews.comment: Taking severity from the report rather than the owner is the right default. That negotiation happens too often.

prompts.title: Operational incident post-mortem
prompts.description: Structures an operational incident into causes, control failures and actions the risk forum can track.
prompts.repetition: Replaces an unstructured incident write-up
prompts.narrative: Incidents produce control changes rather than explanations.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.

tutorial.title: Writing a post-mortem that changes something

inputs.label: Control documentation
inputs.note: Controls that should have caught it

guidelines: Root cause analysis is about controls, not individuals. Never name a person in the output.
A control that worked but was too slow is still a control failure — record it as one.
Actions without an owner and a date do not belong in the forum paper.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are conducting an operational incident review at MUFG.

INPUT: {{INCIDENT TIMELINE}}, {{CONTROL DOCUMENTATION}}
IMPACT: {{LOSS DATA}}

TASK
1. Timeline: what happened, when it was detected, when it was contained
2. Controls that should have prevented it, and how each failed
3. Root cause, distinguished from contributing factors
4. Detection gap: how long between occurrence and detection, and why
5. Actions with owner, date and the control they strengthen

CONSTRAINTS
- Never name an individual. Describe roles and controls.
- Distinguish root cause from contributing factors explicitly.
- Every action must name the control it changes.
prompts.sample_output:
INCIDENT REVIEW — payment routing error

TIMELINE     Occurred 14:20, detected 09:10 next day, contained 11:45
DETECTION GAP 18h 50m — end-of-day reconciliation runs after cut-off

CONTROL FAILURES
 C-114 four-eyes check — operated, but on the instruction not the routing field
 C-118 automated validation — rule did not cover intermediary bank changes

ROOT CAUSE    Validation rule scope, not the manual check
CONTRIBUTING  Reconciliation timing, volume peak

reviews.name: Grace Alden
reviews.comment: Separating root cause from contributing factors stops the post-mortem blaming the last person in the chain.

prompts.title: Sanctions screening rule review
prompts.description: Reviews screening rules for coverage gaps against current sanctions designations.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual rule-by-rule coverage check
prompts.narrative: Designation changes reach the screening engine within the week.
prompts.risk_note: Deal-sensitive or control-facing. Restricted to a cleared team; every run is logged and reviewable by Compliance.
guidelines: No rule change reaches production without Financial Crime Compliance approval and testing.
Coverage gaps are reportable — do not hold one pending a fix.
Never include live customer or transaction data in the input.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a financial crime risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{SCREENING RULES}}, {{DESIGNATION CHANGES}}
SYSTEM: {{TARGET SYSTEM}}

TASK
1. Designations not covered by any current rule
2. Rules whose matching logic would miss a known alias or transliteration
3. Ownership and control cases (50% rule) not captured
4. Proposed rule changes, with expected alert volume impact
5. Anything constituting a reportable coverage gap

CONSTRAINTS
- Flag reportable gaps immediately and separately; do not bundle them.
- Estimate alert volume impact for every proposed change.
- No live customer or transaction data.
prompts.sample_output:
SCREENING COVERAGE REVIEW

REPORTABLE GAP — 2 designations added 4 Aug not covered by any active rule
  Escalated to FCC on generation

Alias coverage   3 rules use exact match only; transliteration variants missed
50% rule         Ownership chains through 2 intermediate entities not captured

PROPOSED CHANGES  4 rules | expected alert volume +14% (ops capacity check needed)

reviews.name: Isaac Kendrick
reviews.comment: Separating reportable gaps from the improvement list is right. Those two things move at completely different speeds.

prompts.title: Correspondent bank risk review
prompts.description: Assesses a correspondent banking relationship against financial crime and country risk criteria.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual annual review per relationship
prompts.narrative: Correspondent reviews are consistent across every relationship in the network.
prompts.risk_note: Deal-sensitive or control-facing. Restricted to a cleared team; every run is logged and reviewable by Compliance.
guidelines: A completed questionnaire is a claim, not evidence. Note where nothing corroborates it.
Nested relationships are the principal risk — check for them explicitly.
Exit recommendations go to the Financial Crime committee, never direct to the business.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are reviewing a correspondent banking relationship at MUFG.

INPUT: {{WOLFSBERG QUESTIONNAIRE}}, {{TRANSACTION PATTERNS}}, {{COUNTRY RISK}}

TASK
1. Respondent profile: ownership, regulator, sanctions history
2. Questionnaire responses that are unsupported by independent evidence
3. Transaction patterns inconsistent with the stated business profile
4. Nested relationship indicators
5. Overall risk rating with the three factors that drive it

CONSTRAINTS
- Distinguish claimed controls from evidenced controls throughout.
- Flag nesting indicators explicitly, even where inconclusive.
- Any exit recommendation routes to the Financial Crime committee.
prompts.sample_output:
CORRESPONDENT REVIEW — Respondent Bank X

Ownership       60% state, 40% private — private holder UNVERIFIED
Claimed controls 14 of 18 evidenced; sanctions screening frequency CLAIMED ONLY
Pattern mismatch USD flows 3.2x the stated trade finance volume

NESTING INDICATORS: 4 downstream institutions identified in payment fields
RATING: High. Drivers — nesting, unverified ownership, pattern mismatch

reviews.name: Hannah York
reviews.comment: The claimed-versus-evidenced split is the whole review in one line. Questionnaires get taken at face value far too often.

prompts.title: Liquidity coverage commentary
prompts.description: Explains an LCR movement with the flows behind it, in the format the ALCO pack expects.
prompts.repetition: Standardises commentary across the daily liquidity pack
prompts.narrative: Ratio movements come with causes attached before the ALCO meeting.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: State the currency basis; a consolidated LCR movement can hide a single-currency problem.
Attribute the move to flows before commenting on the ratio itself.
Do not describe a ratio above the requirement as comfortable without stating the buffer.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a liquidity risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{LCR OUTPUT}}, {{FLOW DETAIL}}
DATE: {{REPORTING DATE}}

TASK
1. LCR at the date, consolidated and by material currency
2. Movement from the prior period, split between HQLA and net outflows
3. The three largest flow drivers, quantified
4. Any single-currency position materially weaker than consolidated
5. A 120-word ALCO commentary

CONSTRAINTS
- Always state the currency basis with any ratio.
- Attribute movement to flows before commenting on the ratio.
- Never describe a buffer as comfortable without quantifying it.
prompts.sample_output:
LCR COMMENTARY — 11 Aug 2026

Consolidated   142% (prior 149%), buffer 42pts above the 100% requirement
By currency    USD 138% | JPY 161% | EUR 104% ← materially weaker

MOVEMENT       −7pts: HQLA −USD 1.2bn (JGB maturity, not reinvested)
                       Net outflows +USD 0.4bn (corporate deposit runoff)

EUR position warrants ALCO attention despite the consolidated buffer.

reviews.name: Thomas Bradley
reviews.comment: The single-currency check is the value here. A healthy consolidated ratio hides a lot.

prompts.title: CVA exposure commentary
prompts.description: Explains a credit valuation adjustment movement across counterparty and market drivers.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual driver attribution each reporting cycle
prompts.narrative: CVA moves are explained by cause rather than presented as a number.
prompts.risk_note: Operates on documents already held inside the MUFG boundary. No external transmission.
guidelines: Separate market-driven moves from portfolio changes; blending them makes the attribution useless.
State the spread source and whether proxies were used for unquoted names.
Proxy spread methodology changes must be disclosed in the commentary.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are an XVA risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{CVA OUTPUT}}, {{CREDIT SPREADS}}, {{TRADE CHANGES}}

TASK
1. CVA movement for the period, total and by counterparty tier
2. Attribution: credit spread moves, market factor moves, trade population,
   collateral changes
3. Counterparties where a proxy spread was used, and their contribution
4. A 150-word commentary for the market risk report

CONSTRAINTS
- Separate market-driven from portfolio-driven movement.
- Identify every proxy spread and its methodology.
- State the netting and collateral assumptions applied.
prompts.sample_output:
CVA MOVEMENT — July 2026

Total CVA   USD 148m (prior 121m), +USD 27m

ATTRIBUTION
  Credit spreads       +USD 19m (widening, IG names)
  Market factors       +USD 6m  (rates, FX)
  Trade population     +USD 4m  (new long-dated swaps)
  Collateral           −USD 2m

PROXY SPREADS: 11 counterparties, contributing USD 8m — sector/rating proxy

reviews.name: Laura Whitman
reviews.comment: Proxy spread contribution as a separate line is a good discipline. That is where the uncertainty actually sits.

prompts.title: Collateral haircut review
prompts.description: Reviews haircuts applied to collateral against market volatility and liquidity conditions.
prompts.repetition: Replaces a manual asset-class-by-asset-class review
prompts.narrative: Haircuts reflect current market liquidity rather than the last calibration.
prompts.risk_note: Handles client or portfolio data. Mask identifiers before upload — the prompt stops if it detects an unmasked account number.
guidelines: Haircut changes are a business decision with client impact — this review informs, it does not implement.
Liquidity conditions matter as much as volatility. A stable price with no bid is not low risk.
Concentration within an asset class needs its own add-on; the standard haircut does not cover it.
prompts.body:
ROLE: You are a collateral risk analyst at MUFG.

INPUT: {{COLLATERAL INVENTORY}}, {{HAIRCUT SCHEDULE}}, {{VOLATILITY DATA}}

TASK
1. Applied haircut versus volatility-implied haircut by asset class
2. Asset classes where liquidity has deteriorated regardless of volatility
3. Concentration within an asset class requiring an add-on
4. Ranked list of haircuts to review, with the reason for each

CONSTRAINTS
- Assess liquidity separately from volatility; do not conflate them.
- Identify concentration positions above the single-issuer threshold.
- Recommend for review; do not implement or imply a change is agreed.
prompts.sample_output:
HAIRCUT REVIEW — 9 asset classes

Corporate bonds, BBB   Applied 8% | Vol-implied 11% | UNDER-HAIRCUT
  Liquidity: bid-ask widened 40% over 3 months — compounding factor
Equities, large cap     Applied 15% | Vol-implied 13% | adequate
Covered bonds           Applied 4%  | vol stable, but LIQUIDITY DETERIORATED

CONCENTRATION: single issuer 22% of corporate bond collateral — add-on needed

reviews.name: Yvonne Hadley
reviews.comment: The liquidity-versus-volatility separation is the right call. Stable prices with no depth is the trap.
